e.t: This Hebrew word describes being strongly attracted to or infatuated with someone, expressing an intense desire that can become misplaced or excessive. In its Old Testament uses, it functions as a verb describing this kind of passionate attachment, especially toward lovers. It occurs eight times in seven Old Testament verses, mainly in Ezekiel 23, with one occurrence in Jeremiah 4:30. The repeated rendering “doted” captures the word’s sense of being deeply captivated, while its use with lovers highlights desire directed toward people rather than a general feeling of admiration.

The name appears eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including genealogical records in Genesis and 1 Chronicles and references connected with Job and Lamentations. Its exact identification—whether a particular ancestor, land, or region—depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic function is to designate Uz by name.

The name appears seven times in the Hebrew Bible corpus, including passages in Joshua, 1 Samuel, 2 Chronicles, Nehemiah, and Jeremiah. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its role in the account.

This Hebrew word means “upper.” It describes something located in an elevated position and functions as a descriptive word for a place or thing. In the Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Joshua 15:19 and Judges 1:15. Its basic sense is limited and clear: it identifies what belongs to an upper location or level. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being described, but the word itself points to its position as upper rather than lower.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “strong.” It describes something possessing strength, firmness, or force rather than weakness. Its normal function is to identify a quality of strength. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 41:21, so Scripture provides only one recorded setting for this word. The precise force intended in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense is strength or being strong.

Pedahzur is a personal name, preserved in English by the rendering “Pedahzur.” It identifies the same person throughout its Hebrew Old Testament occurrences rather than expressing a general action, quality, or object. The name occurs eight times, all in Numbers, across five verses. Its uses appear from Numbers 1 through Numbers 10, so its basic function is to identify a biblical individual in those passages, while the surrounding verse supplies the person’s specific role or connection.

This rare Hebrew word refers to a sharp, cutting edge or implement. It appears only twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Psalm 149:6 and Isaiah 41:15. In both places, it is connected with language describing something equipped or used for cutting, helping define the word’s practical sense. Its exact nuance depends on the surrounding wording in each passage, but the central idea is a sharp, effective cutting edge.

e.h: A Hebrew Word for a Vail
e.t: This Hebrew noun means a “vail,” a covering used in the tabernacle and temple to separate or screen sacred areas. It is associated with the sanctuary’s inner arrangement and with the commanded construction of the dwelling place. The word occurs 25 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in Exodus and Leviticus, showing its repeated use for this sacred furnishing rather than for an ordinary household covering. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description of the sanctuary.

It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Daniel 6:17, so its normal lexical sense is limited to that single occurrence. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is purpose: what is intended or meant to be carried out.

In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 33:7. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise force in that verse must be understood from the wider context, but its central sense is a person marked by valor and courage.

e.t: This Hebrew verb means “smell.” It describes the action associated with smelling and is used in the Old Testament in statements involving scent. The word occurs 11 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Amos. Its ordinary sense is identified primarily through its repeated English rendering, while the surrounding verse determines how the action operates in that particular sentence. It should therefore be understood as a verb expressing “smell,” rather than as a general noun for a scent or fragrance.

Its uses include descriptions associated with thunderous sound, but the word’s central idea is the producing or expressing of a roar. It occurs 13 times in the Old Testament, so its precise force depends on the sentence where it appears.

e.t: Rithmah is a place name, referring to a location in the Israelites’ wilderness journey. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Numbers 33, where the journey’s stopping places are listed. Because the name is preserved rather than translated, it identifies the location itself instead of expressing an action, quality, or teaching. Its exact setting and significance must be understood from the surrounding passage, but the word’s ordinary function is simply to name a place.

This Hebrew word means “plenteous.” It describes a condition marked by a great amount, especially when referring to a season or yield. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs eight times, including six occurrences in Genesis 41 and later occurrences in Proverbs and Ecclesiastes. Its use in Genesis 41 is rendered “plenteous,” supporting the sense of more than enough. The surrounding verse determines what is plenteous.

This Hebrew word means “excellency,” referring to a state of elevated standing or distinction. It functions as a noun, naming the quality or condition of being exalted. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Bible corpus, in Job 20:6, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its connection with terms related to rising and the head supports the idea of something raised to a high position, rather than an ordinary or low condition.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a garment, meaning an item of clothing worn or used to cover the body. It functions as a noun and can describe ordinary clothing in different situations, including clothing that is given, worn, or becomes worn with time. The word occurs 16 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a consistent reference to clothing rather than to a person or action. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

“Shimrith” is a Hebrew personal name, referring to one individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at 2 Chronicles 24:26, and English renderings preserve it as “Shimrith.” Because this word functions as a name, its ordinary meaning is identification: it distinguishes the person who bears it. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain that person’s role in the passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “generations,” referring to a succession of descendants as a family line unfolds. It functions as a noun for people connected through birth and begetting, and it can frame the continuation of a family line across time. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 39 times, beginning in Genesis and continuing through 1 Chronicles. Its use also appears near creation language, linking what God made with the generations that followed.

e.t: Oboth is a Hebrew proper name rendered as “Oboth,” referring to a named place in the Old Testament. It is not presented here as a general descriptive word or an action; its role is to identify a location. The name occurs four times, all in Numbers, in references describing Israel’s journey and camping locations. Because no broader definition or verse text is available, the clearest meaning is simply the place-name Oboth.

e.t: The Hebrew word means “behemoth.” It refers to a particular being identified by this name rather than expressing an action, quality, or instruction. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Job 40:15, so its use is limited to that passage. English translations preserve the term as “behemoth” instead of replacing it with a more familiar descriptive word. Its precise role in Job 40:15 depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which must be considered separately from this word’s basic meaning.
